title: 따로 만나는 거 그만하자  (Let's Stop Meeting Privately)

segments.t: Stepping onto the night sidewalk outside the noisy restaurant, Ra Joon-mo runs into assistant director Shin Hye-joo, whom he has been casually seeing without real commitment. Stung by Youn Yuh-jung's scolding about honesty, Joon-mo decides to end things clearly and politely instead of vanishing. Listen for "ibyeol", 'a breakup', and "geumanhaja", 'let's stop'.
혜주야, 나 너한테 할 말 있다.
우리는 네가 원하는 관계가 될 순 없을 것 같아.
Let's go through Joon-mo's quiet talk outside the restaurant step by step.

'I actually just stepped out to call you.' Hye-joo opens with "an geuraedo", a handy conversational bridge meaning 'as a matter of fact' or 'just as you showed up', before "jeonhwaharyeogo", 'intending to phone'.

'Inside is chaotic like a marketplace. Let's slip out separately.' Calling a loud room "sijangtong", 'a bustling street market', is vivid everyday Korean. "Ttaro" means 'apart from the crowd' or 'just the two of us'.
혜주야, 나 너한테 할 말 있다.
'Hye-joo, I have something to say to you.' Adding "-ya" to a name ending in a vowel is friendly casual address, while "hal mal itda" signals serious news: 'I have something I need to tell you'.
'Yes? What is it?' Sensing the shift in mood, Hye-joo switches to polite "ne" and asks "museun mariyo", using "museun" for 'what kind of'.

'When something doesn't feel right, a person should say so clearly.' Remembering how badly hints went inside, Joon-mo chooses "hwaksilhage", 'unmistakably' or 'clearly', alongside "yaegihaeyaji", 'one ought to speak up'.
'Even in a breakup, there is such a thing as courtesy.' Here "ibyeol" means 'parting ways', and "yeui" is 'good manners' or 'decency' — echoing the exact lesson he heard earlier in the day.
'You're nice and pretty, though.' He softens the blow with "joko", 'kind and likable', and spoken "ippeugin hande", 'you certainly are pretty, but...', leaving the contrast hanging gently.
우리는 네가 원하는 관계가 될 순 없을 것 같아.

'I don't think we can become the kind of relationship you want.' "Wonhaneun" means 'wishing for', modifying "gwangye", 'relationship', while "eopsseul geot gata" softens 'cannot become' into 'it seems we cannot'.
'Pardon?' Caught off guard, Hye-joo lets out a quiet, rising "ne?" — the polite way to ask 'what did you just say?'.
'Let's stop meeting on our own.' Rather than ghosting her, Joon-mo states it plainly: "ttaro mannaneun geo", 'seeing each other privately', plus "geumanhaja", 'let's call it off'.
'I'm sorry.' With a younger colleague he knows well, Joon-mo uses plain "mianhada", sincere and unadorned.

'I understand, senior.' Taking a quiet breath, Hye-joo answers "algesseoyo", a calm 'got it, I understand', addressing him simply as "seonbae". Now let's hear the entire sidewalk conversation again from top to bottom.
혜주야, 나 너한테 할 말 있다.
우리는 네가 원하는 관계가 될 순 없을 것 같아.
You just picked up "an geuraedo" for natural transitions, "hwaksilhage" for speaking clearly, and "geumanhaja" when it is time to wrap something up. Until next time!

lines.fragment: 혜주야 나 너한테 할 말 있다
관계가 될 순 없을 것 같아
